[FARRA:v1p333/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Arabic uses a direct reflexive expression with complete verbs (قتلتم أنفسكم; ظلموا أنفسهم), but defective cognition verbs take a pronoun attached to the verb (أظنني خارجا), distinguishing verbs that may be omitted from those that cannot.
[FARRA:v1p333/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The Qurʾān says أن رآه استغنى rather than رأى نفسه; poetry can use a direct object with a complete verb, but forms such as عدمتني are not standard speech.
[FARRA:v3p278/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The self pronoun is omitted in “when he saw himself self-sufficient”: Arabic supplies it with reflexive actions, and can drop it when the verb has a predicate.
[FARRA:v3p278/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Arabic says “when do you see yourself going out?” or “when do you think yourself going out?” with nafs omitted before a predicate.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p534#2/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | A human being transgresses when he sees himself as self-sufficient.
[TAB:96:6/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | It is wrong for a person to receive God's gifts of sound creation, knowledge, and unmatched favor, then disbelieve and transgress against Him. | mentions 96:7
[TAB:96:6/r2] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The human oversteps bounds, grows arrogant toward God, and disbelieves because he sees himself as self-sufficient. | mentions 96:7
[TAB:96:6/r3] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | In grammar, raʾā takes a subject and predicate, so Arabs use a self-referential pronoun plus a second complement; verbs taking one object instead take an explicit reflexive noun.
[TAB:96:7/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | ‘Kalla’ rebukes a human who receives God's gifts of sound creation, knowledge, and unmatched favors, then disbelieves and transgresses against Him upon seeing himself self-sufficient. | mentions 96:6
[TAB:96:7/r2] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The human exceeds his limits and arrogantly disbelieves in his Lord because he sees himself as self-sufficient.
[TAB:96:7/r3] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The construction treats the reflexive pronoun as the subject and ‘self-sufficient’ as the predicate because raʾā needs both; Arabic uses similar forms with verbs like ‘consider,’ but a verb taking one object instead uses a reflexive object such as ‘you killed yourself.’
[TAB-FULL:v24p533/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Humans transgress and grow arrogant toward God, disbelieving when they see themselves as self-sufficient; Ṭabarī also explains Arabic reflexive phrasing for seeing oneself.
[TAB-FULL:v24p533/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The verb raʾā here takes a subject and predicate, so Arabs use a reflexive pronoun when the speaker makes the self the object; a verb taking only one object instead uses nafsaka.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p345/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | These verses were revealed concerning Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, who threatened to trample Muhammad's neck if he saw him praying.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p692/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · ابن كثير عن قنبل | reports | Ibn Kathīr as read by Qunbul omits the alif after hamza in رآه; Ibn Mujāhid calls this mistaken, since the word parallels رعاه with or without imāla.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p692/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr reads رآه with fatḥa on rāʾ and kasra on hamza.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p692/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · ابن عامر وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر وحمزة والكسائي | reports | These readers break rāʾ and lengthen an open hamza; Nāfiʿ and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read both relevant vowels open.
[IBNABIHATIM:v10p3450#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud says two people are insatiable—the scholar and the worldly person; they differ because the scholar gains God's approval while the worldly person persists in transgression, linking these verses with the verse about learned fear. | mentions 35:28

[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p423/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن عامر وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر وحمزة والكسائي | reports | These readers pronounce رآه with imāla of the rāʾ toward kasra and retain the alif after hamza.

[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p423/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The report of rāʾ with kasra means imāla of its fatḥa; some trusted readers also imale the rāʾ, hamza, and alif.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p423/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Deleting the long alif from a past-tense form cannot be inferred from rare deletions in an irregular imperfect; such deletion is not analogical. | mentions 12:31

[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p423/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The poet's من را is not like Ibn Kathīr's reading: the poet metathesized hamza and then deleted after two consonants met, while the reading articulates hamza fully.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p425/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | A poetic form أري عيني ما لم ترأياه preserves the hamza, then deletes it for the jussive and eases it as in المرأة and الكمأة.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p425/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In أن رآه, أن introduces a subject-and-predicate clause, as shown by the attached pronoun; استغنى is its second object.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p425/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Imāla moves from the hamza to the preceding rāʾ as it does from an imaled alif; Nāfiʿ and Ḥafṣ leave it open, while Abū ʿAmr opens rāʾ but imales hamza.
[SULAMI:v2p407#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Seeing oneself as wealthy breeds tyranny and arrogance through pride.
[SULAMI:v2p407#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · يحيى بن معاذ | reports | Knowledge and wealth each produce tyranny; asceticism protects from tyranny in worship, and persistent hunger helps reach asceticism by cutting desire for sin.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p171#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | “The human” is Abū Jahl; his transgression was that when wealthy he upgraded his clothes, mount, food, and drink. Al-Kalbī similarly describes him rising in status through dress and food.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p172/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | He sees himself as wealthy and so transgresses; God warns him of his return to Him.
